title: Drive a curved suture needle through a practice pad and pass it to the other hand
instruction: Drive the curved needle through the practice pad as a surgeon does: turn it about the centre of its curve so that it follows its own path, going in through the slot right of the cut and out through the slot left of the cut. Then take hold of the needle where it has come out with your other hand, and let go of it with the first.
context: Driving a curved needle through tissue is the basic move of suturing: surgeons repeat it many times in every operation, and trainees drill it on silicone practice pads. The wrist turns the needle about the centre of its curve, so that its body follows the track its tip has cut; pushed straight or levered, it drags sideways through its entry and exit holes and tears them, which surgical skill assessments score as poor respect for tissue. Once the tip has come out, the other hand takes the needle on the part that has come through, and the first hand lets go while the needle still runs through both holes, so it is never pulled back or dropped. Done by: surgeons, surgical residents, physician assistants and nurse practitioners, and the instructors who train them on suture pads.
setup: On the table, in front of the arms: a suture practice pad standing upright on a grey aluminium stand (18.6 x 5.8 x 1 cm), turned 30 degrees clockwise seen from above, so that its skin faces back toward the left arm and its right end is nearer the arms. The pad is a hollow skin-coloured silicone block, 17 cm wide, 4 cm deep and 8 cm tall, with 5 mm walls; its front face, the skin, is a 4 mm silicone plate with a vertical cut drawn down its middle (a dark red line 5 mm wide and 4.4 cm long) and an open slot on each side of the cut, 18 mm tall and running from 2.4 to 5.7 cm from the cut, centred 6 cm above the table. Its centre (on the cut, at the slots' height) is 29.6 cm in front of the arm bases and 2.1 cm right of the midline. The needle is a blunt grey half circle of solid PLA, 6 cm radius and 9 mm square in section, 19 g, with a dark tip and a blue band at its back end. It lies flat on a white foam block (5 cm front to back, 10 cm side to side, 5.6 cm tall, centred 11.4 cm in front of the arm bases and 6.0 cm right of the midline), its arc bowing toward the arms: its tip is 16 cm in front of the arm bases and 12 cm right of the midline, its back end 16 cm in front on the midline, and the middle of its arc 10 cm in front. The pad and the block are fixed; the needle is loose.
scoring: A hole is torn when the point where the needle's centreline crosses the skin's front face moves more than 4 mm sideways along the skin (horizontally, toward or away from the cut) from where it first crossed there. A hand holds the needle when its fingers have closed onto its section (the finger pads 7 to 11.5 mm apart) and its axis passes within 6 mm of the needle's centreline; a hand has let go when its axis is 2 cm or more from the needle's centreline. The hand that drove it in is the one holding it when the tip passes behind the cut (if both are, the one further back on the needle; if neither, the last to hold it, or else the nearest). Score 0 if, at any time: a hole is torn; the needle crosses the skin outside a slot; a finger pad comes within 1 mm of the pad (pressing the tissue); or the needle is dropped (no hand holds it and all of its centreline is 3 cm or more below the slots' height). Otherwise the levels build on each other and are kept once reached: 0.25 when the tip has gone in through the slot right of the cut and been driven behind the cut; 0.5 when, also, it has come out through the slot left of the cut with at least 2 cm of needle out; 0.75 when, also, the other hand holds the needle on the part that has come out; 1.0 when, also, the other hand still holds it there, the hand that drove it in has let go, the needle still runs through both slots and it has been still for 1 s (its arc's centre moving less than 1 mm); held for 1 s, this ends the trial with success. Doing nothing scores 0.
reset_notes: Lay the needle back on its foam block as at the start. Run with -E object_jitter=0: the layout, the scoring and the scripted demo depend on it. For real trials, build the same slotted pad and tape a strip of tissue paper over the front of each slot for the needle to poke through. After the trial, measure each paper slit's horizontal length with calipers: a correctly turned needle leaves about 12.7 mm (its 9 mm section crosses the skin at a slant), so a slit longer than 16.7 mm is a torn hole. Film from above to check the order of entry and exit and the hand-off.
fidelity: Approximate. The needle is rigid and about 6 times real size (6 cm radius, 9 mm thick) so the 15 mm finger pads can hold it. Tissue isn't simulated: open slots stand in for the holes a needle punches, and a hole counts as torn when the needle's crossing point moves more than 4 mm sideways along the skin; up-and-down movement in the 18 mm slots isn't scored. There is no thread, and the needle isn't pulled all the way through: the task ends when its tip has been handed to the other hand.
